questions.stem: What is the centre of gravity (G) of a vessel?
options: The centre of the underwater volume of the hull
The single point through which the whole weight of the vessel and everything aboard acts downward
The point on the centreline at the height of the waterline
The point where the upward line through B meets the centreline
questions.explanation: G is the balance point of all the weights aboard. The centre of the underwater volume is B, the centre of buoyancy. The waterline height has nothing to do with it, and the point where the upward line through B meets the centreline is the metacentre M.

questions.stem: What is the centre of buoyancy (B)?
options: The centre of the weight of the vessel
The centre of the waterplane area at the waterline
The centre of the underwater volume of the hull, through which the whole upward buoyant force acts
The highest point of the hull's underwater shape
questions.explanation: B is the geometric centre of the underwater volume, and the buoyant force equal to the displacement acts up through it. The centre of weight is G. It is not the centre of the waterplane area or the top of the underwater shape.

questions.stem: A vessel with nothing shifting heels over a few degrees to starboard. What happens to G and to B?
options: G stays where it is; B moves toward the starboard (low) side
B stays where it is; G moves toward the starboard side
Both G and B move toward the port (high) side
G rises and B falls
questions.explanation: Heeling does not move any weight, so G stays. The underwater shape changes, with more hull immersed on the low side, so B moves toward the side that went down. That puts the upward force off to the low side of the downward force and creates the righting turn.

questions.stem: At a small angle of heel, which is the metacentre (M)?
options: The point where the vertical line up through G meets the keel
The centre of the vessel's underwater volume
The point where the vertical line up through the new B cuts the original centreline
The point through which all the weight acts
questions.explanation: M is found by drawing the upward buoyancy line through the new B and seeing where it crosses the centreline; for small angles it stays almost fixed. The keel point is K, the underwater centre is B, and the weight point is G.

questions.stem: M is below G in a vessel that is upright in still water. What kind of equilibrium is she in, and what will happen?
options: Unstable equilibrium; she will not stay upright and will heel over to an angle of loll or capsize
Stable equilibrium; she will return to upright after a push
Neutral equilibrium; she will stay at any angle she is left at
Stable equilibrium, but only in calm water
questions.explanation: M below G means negative GM. The upward line through B passes on the high side of G and pushes the vessel further over, like a marble balanced on a dome. Stable needs M above G, and neutral needs M at G.

questions.stem: A vessel's GM is exactly zero. Which description fits?
options: Stable equilibrium, with a weak turning effect back to upright
Unstable equilibrium, with a turning effect that pushes it further over
She is safe, because zero means no heel
Neutral equilibrium: it stays at whatever small angle it is pushed to, with no turning effect either way
questions.explanation: With M at G the two forces stay in line at every small angle, so there is no righting or capsizing turn: neutral equilibrium. That is a dangerous place to be, because the slightest further rise of G makes her unstable. Zero GM does not mean there is no heel.

questions.stem: An invented box-shaped barge is 8.0 m long and 3.0 m wide and floats at a draught of 0.80 m. Using KB = half the draught and BM = I / V with I = L x B^3 / 12, what is KM?
options: About 0.94 m
About 1.34 m
About 0.40 m
About 1.74 m
questions.explanation: V = 8.0 x 3.0 x 0.80 = 19.2 m3. I = 8.0 x 27 / 12 = 18.0 m4. BM = 18.0 / 19.2 = 0.9375 m. KB = 0.40 m. KM = KB + BM = 1.3375 m, about 1.34 m. 0.94 m is BM alone (KB left out) and 0.40 m is KB alone. 1.74 m uses the whole draught (0.80 m) as KB instead of half of it.

questions.stem: Two barges have the same length and draught, but the second is twice as wide as the first. Compared with the first, how does the second barge's BM compare?
options: Twice as large
Four times larger
Eight times larger
The same
questions.explanation: I = L x B^3 / 12 grows with the cube of the breadth, so doubling the breadth makes I eight times larger. The underwater volume V only doubles, so BM = I / V is 8 / 2 = 4 times larger. Eight is the increase in I, not BM, and twice would ignore the cube.

questions.stem: Which is the most common cause of lost stability on small vessels?
options: A fall in KB as the vessel heels
Making the beam wider
Lowering the freeboard by painting the hull
Raising KG, for example by stowing weight high or adding top weight
questions.explanation: KM comes from the hull shape and draught and changes little in service, whereas KG changes every time weight is added, moved or burned. A rising KG cuts GM, so top weight is the usual culprit. A wider beam increases BM and helps stability.
